articles.title: Spain’s 2026 election explained in maps and charts
articles.summary: Spaniards vote on November 29 in a snap general election. Here is how the system works, the parties and the key issues.
articles.body:
Spain will hold a snap election on November 29 that could bring the far right into government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1975.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the early vote last month after parliament rejected his government’s housing relief measures, which came during mass protests over rents and house prices.

Polls suggest the centre-right People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party to reach the 176 seats required for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Voters will also elect 208 members of the Senate.

About 38.7 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute (INE).

Polling stations across Spain will be open on November 29 at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT).

Spain is a parliamentary monarchy. King Felipe VI is head of state, while the government is led by a prime minister who answers to the Cortes Generales, a parliament made up of two houses: the Congress of Deputies and the Senate.

The 350 members of the lower house, the Congress of Deputies, are elected in 52 constituencies by proportional representation. Rather than choosing individual candidates, voters pick a party, and each party puts forward a ranked list of candidates in every constituency.

Every province is guaranteed at least two seats and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa get one each. The rest are distributed by population, which is why Madrid and Barcelona elect far more deputies than smaller provinces.

Within each constituency, seats are divided according to each party’s share of the vote and go to the candidates at the top of each list. A party needs at least 3 percent of the vote in a constituency to qualify for any seats there.

A party needs 176 of the 350 seats for a majority. If no party reaches that number, parties must form coalitions or strike deals to govern. After consulting party leaders, the king proposes a candidate for prime minister, who must then win an investiture vote in Congress.

Most members of the upper house, the Senate, are elected directly, with voters choosing individual candidates by name. In most provinces, each voter can back up to three candidates and the four with the most votes are elected. The remaining senators are appointed by Spain’s regional parliaments.

Provisional results from the Interior Ministry will start coming in straight away, with the overall picture clear before midnight on Sunday.

In 2023, about 99 percent of votes had been counted by 11:45pm.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority coalition government made up of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and the left-wing Sumar alliance. The 22-member cabinet comprises Sanchez, three deputy prime ministers and 18 other ministers.

The three deputy prime ministers each oversee a major policy area: Carlos Cuerpo oversees the economy, Yolanda Diaz labour and the social economy and Sara Aagesen the ecological transition. Cuerpo is also acting transport minister after Oscar Puente resigned after last month’s train crash that killed 69 people.

Thirteen cabinet members belong to the PSOE and five to Sumar, while four are independents appointed by the PSOE.

Which are the main parties on the ballot?

Socialist Party (PSOE), centre-left – Incumbent Pedro Sanchez is running again after more than eight years in office, which makes him Spain’s second-longest-serving prime minister since 1978, after Felipe Gonzalez. His final two years in power were overshadowed by corruption investigations involving his wife, his brother and former close allies.

People’s Party (PP), centre-right – Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has led the PP since 2022, is the party’s candidate. The PP won the most seats in the 2023 election but could not gather enough support to form a government.

Vox, far right – Led by Santiago Abascal, who co-founded the party in 2014 after leaving the PP, Vox has become Spain’s third-largest party. It campaigns for tougher immigration rules, lower taxes and a hard line against Catalan and Basque separatism.

Broad Front (Frente Amplio), left – Headed by Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona, it is a new alliance that replaces Sumar, the left-wing grouping that has governed alongside Sanchez since 2023. Podemos, a former partner of Sumar, is running separately.

Regional parties – Could again decide who governs. EH Bildu (Basque Country), the BNG (Galicia), the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) and the left-wing Catalan pro-independence ERC have largely backed Sanchez. The centre-right Catalan pro-independence party Junts supported his 2023 investiture but has since repeatedly voted against his government.

According to a YouGov poll published on October 30 , the main issues according to the Spanish public are:

Housing – Spain is short of 750,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain, which warns that the gap could surpass one million by 2028. The average rent has reached 1,176 euros ($1,318) a month, almost exactly a young person’s average monthly salary of 1,191 euros ($1,334), according to the Spanish Youth Council. Anger over housing costs has fuelled nationwide protests .

Immigration – Sanchez has been one of Europe’s leading advocates of migration and this year offered undocumented migrants a path to legal status, drawing almost 1.2 million applications. Vox, on the other hand, has pledged to deport all undocumented migrants, while the PP has promised tighter border controls in its manifesto.

Corruption – Sanchez is facing up to nine judicial investigations involving his party, government and family. His former transport minister Jose Luis Abalos was sentenced to 24 years in prison for corruption in June. Opposition parties have put corruption at the centre of their campaigns and accuse Sanchez’s government of being mired in scandal.

Healthcare – Long waiting lists are a growing concern across Spain. Doctors have postponed a national strike over working-hours reforms until after the election, but regional walkouts continue.

State of the economy – Spain’s economy has grown faster than the eurozone average, but inflation near 5 percent and soaring housing costs mean many Spaniards are not feeling the benefits.

articles.title: Ranking the top 5 GOP candidates for president
articles.summary: Before November’s midterm elections, the 2028 Republican presidential primary was viewed largely as a race between two men who would carry President Trump’s legacy forward: Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But after the GOP’s disastrous performance earlier this month, when Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate, Republicans are…
articles.body:
Before November’s midterm elections, the 2028 Republican presidential primary was viewed largely as a race between two men who would carry President Trump’s legacy forward: Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

But after the GOP’s disastrous performance earlier this month, when Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate, Republicans are considering a broader field of would-be contenders.

Some Republicans who may not have wanted to run against Vance or Rubio are now considering their options in what is increasingly viewed as a wide-open race to succeed the current president.

Yet Trump is also a problem of sorts for those thinking of running for the GOP presidential nomination.

The president’s policies were seen as a drag on the GOP in the midterms. Now a lame-duck president, his rhetoric and policy will nonetheless loom large over the presidential race, shaping the landscape and potentially pigeonholing candidates who might want some freedom and daylight from the White House on the campaign trail.

Here’s a snapshot of the top five likely Republican candidates at this early stage of the race.

While he’s still largely seen as the heir apparent to Trump, the vice president’s political aspirations have become increasingly complex and muddied since the midterms.

As Republicans increasingly look to turn the page and possibly move away from the Trump era, Vance’s proximity to the president — once seen as a huge strength for his presidential prospects — may now be in danger of becoming a disadvantage.

Vance has seemingly attempted to create some space from Trump on issues such as the war in Iran, but it will be difficult for him to do this without feeling the president’s wrath.

Over the past two weeks, Vance allies have suggested he is considering not running in 2028, a move that would completely open up the race on the Republican side.

Other allies say the vice president is still undecided on a presidential run.

“He has some time to figure things out in the coming weeks,” one GOP operative said. “I imagine that decision won’t be easy.”

The political chatter about a potential Rubio candidacy has reached a near fever pitch since the midterms, when Republicans began to openly wonder if Vance was the right candidate for 2028.

Rubio has also surged ahead of Vance in an Emerson poll out this month, which showed that the secretary of State had 36 percent support among Republican primary voters, while Vance had 20 percent — a reversal from a year ago.

Just a week ago, Vance and Rubio both appeared with Trump at the White House press podium, underscoring the rivalry between the two.

It’s not entirely clear whether Rubio wants to run for the White House.

Rubio has long said he would defer to Vance should the vice president decide to run. Allies also say Rubio wants to enter the private sector to make some money, interrupting a government career.

Others think Rubio would run, but he doesn’t want to be seen as campaigning for the role. There’s open talk about the idea of drafting him into the presidential race.

And then there are allies of Rubio who say he will enter the race “if the environment is right.”

While it’s possible Rubio could wait until 2032, there are always risks to doing so if the time to run is now.

“I think he’s very much aware of the pitfalls if he did enter,” one ally said.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) came out of the midterms with a strong argument to make as he considers his political future.

Republicans in his state, DeSantis noted, largely withstood the blue wave that took down Republicans in Georgia, Texas and the Carolinas.

Even before the results came in, DeSantis said Republicans delivered the wrong message to voters during the midterm campaigns.

In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith earlier this month, he accused some Republicans of “gaslighting” voters when they didn’t fully address the economic anxiety many people were feeling across the country.

As he leaves the governor’s mansion in the coming weeks, DeSantis will have to decide whether his brand of politics is what his party is craving.

“He has a great case to make,” one GOP strategist said. “But the timing may still not be quite right.”

Even before the midterms, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) had begun to create some distance with Trump’s positions.

In the days following the midterms, Cruz has become more vocal about how the war in Iran and Trump’s tariff policies hurt Republicans.

It’s created an opening for him to show that he’s trying to bring a new era to the Republican Party.

He has also sought to differentiate himself from Vance on foreign policy issues, and he has pushed back on the vice president’s America-first positions.

Earlier this month, while appearing at the Jewish Leadership Conference in New York, Cruz took issue with Vance’s views that public dissatisfaction with the country’s relationship with Israel was one of the reasons Republicans lost.

“Anyone who looks at this election and sees a mandate to abandon Israel is seeing something I certainly don’t see, and I certainly don’t agree,” he said, according to Jewish Insider.

But even GOP operatives wonder how far Cruz can navigate outside the administration’s stances without angering Trump and his loyal base.

Some Republicans have started to make the case that Glenn Youngkin is exactly what the party needs in its rebuilding effort.

They point to the coalition Youngkin put together when he won his gubernatorial race in 2021.

Since leaving office in January, Youngkin has tried to build up his national profile, launching a conservative education policy group, which has poured millions of dollars into advertising in battleground states including Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Michigan.

One Republican strategist said Youngkin was far enough removed from the administration to move the needle.

“A governor like Youngkin could be just what we need right now.”

articles.title: Lutnick in the hot seat as senators vow to crack down on AI chip leaks to China
articles.summary: Senators in both parties say that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in the hot seat in the wake of revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech chips to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy. Lawmakers in both parties criticized President Trump’s intervention…
articles.body:
Senators in both parties say that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in the hot seat in the wake of revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech chips to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy.

Lawmakers in both parties criticized President Trump’s intervention to persuade Nvidia’s board to bring Jensen Huang back as its CEO after he admitted to the extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom American intelligence said had contact with a Chinese spy agency.

But while senators have limited ability to change Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang, they can exert more pressure on Lutnick, whose department depends on appropriations from Congress.

“I think that Mr. Lutnick’s got a host of problems,” said Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the incoming chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee who also sits on the Senate Banking Committee, which will hear testimony from Huang next week.

Warner suggested the Commerce Department may have allowed Nvidia to make sensitive technology sales to companies in addition to Megaspeed, the company connected to Alice Huang, that undermined restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips.

“The idea that the Commerce Department has been allowing potentially not just some of these one-off descriptions of [chip sales] that Nvidia’s been doing but through other Chinese shell companies — we deserve answers,” he said.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the current chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he had warned the Trump administration that advanced chips were getting past export controls and called on Congress to pass legislation to tighten restrictions.

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other,” Cotton posted on the social platform X.

Lutnick is coming under heavy scrutiny from both Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill after media outlets reported that he resisted pressure from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to put Megaspeed, the company previously affiliated with Alice Huang, on a trade blacklist.

Bessent confronted Lutnick earlier this month over why the Commerce Department had not banned the sale of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed, according to The New York Times.

Bessent told CNBC in an interview that he was frustrated over the delay in restricting chip sales and blamed the Commerce Department for not acting.

“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, adding that the Commerce Department “has the pen” and suggesting that it should explain “their internal processes.”

Democrats, who will control the Senate and House in January, are pressing for answers about whether Lutnick may have been motivated by a financial conflict of interest.

They want to know whether data centers in Southeast Asian countries that supplied advanced computing power to China had financial ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm that Lutnick once led and is now run by his sons.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, said Lutnick and other members of the Trump administration may “have converging personal, political, corporate and financial interests in making sure” Jensen Huang remains as Nvidia’s CEO.

Lawmakers want to know what role Lutnick may have played in delaying the implementation of rules to restrict the sale of chips to companies such as Megaspeed and A201, a data center based in Malaysia, that allegedly provided China access to advanced computing power.

The Commerce Department has said Lutnick has complied with all ethics rules.

But key Republicans have joined Democrats in calling on Lutnick to testify about his role overseeing policies and regulations on chip exports.

Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has asked Lutnick to appear before his panel next month to answer questions.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the Commerce Department appeared to “knowingly” allow sensitive AI technology to skirt export restrictions.

“It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying, ‘Stop it.’ So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath,” he said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“If Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” he added.

This has prompted speculation on Capitol Hill that Lutnick’s future leadership of the Commerce Department could be on shaky ground.

Lutnick will have to answer tough questions about a new report in The Atlantic that he transferred federal agents who were tasked with investigating the smuggling of advanced AI chips to his personal security detail, taking those agents off a critical national security job.

Incoming Senate Commerce Committee Chair Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said she has “great concerns about his leadership of Commerce.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said Lutnick should resign amid reports that the Commerce Department slow-walked export controls for AI chips.

Tillis said Lutnick was briefed on the findings by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy before Trump invited the Nvidia CEO to join him on Air Force One in Alaska en route to a trip to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He said Lutnick should have intervened to block Huang from joining the president, something that Rubio tried to do.

“It was my understanding that Lutnick had been briefed on it too. Let’s just say for the sake of argument that the president was distracted and did not remember telling him about it. Lutnick should have damn well should have known,” Tillis said.

He said it was not appropriate for Huang to join Trump on the high-level trip. He also cited what he called Lutnick’s “entanglements with investments in Nvidia.”

Asked if Lutnick should resign, Tillis said: “I think he should roll.”

The Hill reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.

articles.title: How to spot real Black Friday savings this holiday season amid the affordability squeeze
articles.summary: A marketing professor warns that Black Friday deals aren't always real discounts, citing shrinkflation and inflation as factors that obscure true savings.
articles.body: Black Friday deals are everywhere, but a sale price does not always mean real savings. With budgets under pressure, amid a persisting affordability crisis and rising fuel prices with the raging Iran conflict, shoppers are looking for ways to stretch their money during the holiday shopping season this year. The forecasts point to a season of cautious spending. Visa Business and Economics Insights expects holiday sales to increase 4.5% from last year — but after accounting for higher prices, the actual increase in what shoppers buy is projected to be just 1.1%. That makes it all the more important for shoppers to know what they’re paying for and whether a sale is truly a deal. "It's still a good time to shop. It's just that you just have to be a little bit more careful," Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, told Fox News Digital when discussing holiday and Black Friday shopping. 7 HOLIDAY SHOPPING SCAMS TO WATCH FOR THIS SEASON Gauri revealed that shopping during Black Friday does not always produce the best deal — especially when it comes to essential technology like cell phones. He advised shoppers to set a budget and research prices before making a purchase, especially for big-ticket items. "Have a number in mind and do your research before you go about spending the money," he said, recommending price-tracking sites and extra promotions. Gauri cited higher gas prices compared with last year as a potential pressure point for consumers, particularly those considering larger purchases. While the average price of a gallon has risen from approximately $3 in November 2025 to $3.64 per gallon this November, according to AAA, the surging price of diesel is what is impacting the cost of nearly all goods for Americans. GOOGLE'S NEW AI SHOPPING CART TRACKS DEALS ACROSS STORES Tariffs are another potential source of price pressure. A New York Fed analysis found that about 26% of tariff increases from 2025 had been passed on to consumer prices. Retailers may also respond to higher costs by raising prices or reducing package sizes. Gauri said some retailers have done both, a practice known as shrinkflation. "The package size is getting smaller, even though the price might be the same," he said. "You’re shaving off, let’s say, 10% of the product." Gauri said Black Friday promotions now often begin during Thanksgiving week and run through Cyber Monday, giving shoppers more time to compare prices online and in stores. The shift from doorbusters that once drew shoppers to stores before dawn the Friday after Thanksgiving means consumers can now research deals, order products and arrange for pickup or delivery. To make sure a discount is worthwhile, Gauri recommended using price-tracking websites and Amazon’s price-history feature to check what an item has cost in recent months. "Consumers tend to overspend sometimes because they do not remember what an item previously cost," he said. He also advised shoppers to compare prices across retailers and check each store’s price-matching policy before making a major purchase. Some retailers exclude Black Friday specials from those policies, he said. Gauri cautioned that Black Friday is not always the best time to shop. "For cellphones, Black Friday doesn’t get you anything special," he said, adding that the best deals on phones or plans often come in October, around new product launches and carrier promotions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Still, shoppers may find Cyber Week discounts useful for stocking up on everyday essentials. Adobe Analytics projects online sales of clothing basics will run 210% above the September average, while personal hygiene products will be up 150%. Baby products, pet supplies and household cleaning items are also expected to see a boost. With budgets under pressure, Gauri advised shoppers to set a spending limit before heading into the holiday sales.

articles.title: The 2028 presidential election cycle is all about Trump
articles.summary: Looking ahead to the 2028 presidential election, Donald Trump’s influence over potential successors like JD Vance and Marco Rubio continues to shape a highly unpredictable political landscape.
articles.body:
Ever since Donald Trump descended Trump Tower’s golden escalator on June 16, 2015, to announce his presidential intentions, he has dominated the political universe. Eleven years later, as a term-limited, lame-duck president, loath to relinquish power and addicted to media attention, he will try to make the race to succeed him all about him.

Therefore, the 2028 presidential election cycle, President Trump’s last chance to wield power by selecting an heir to cement his legacy, is poised to be uniquely dramatic and unpredictable. No one could have predicted the 2024 presidential election’s out-of-bounds events — Trump’s near-assassination and President Biden’s last-minute withdrawal . So what sort of what-ifs can we reasonably discuss?

What if, by Election Day 2028, Trump is not the incumbent. This is a touchy topic but not a terribly unlikely one. Trump turns 82 in June 2028. Many people pass away at that age. Also, a severe mental or physical health crisis could trigger the 25th Amendment if Trump is “unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office.” That determination rests with Vice President JD Vance and a majority of Trump’s Cabinet, who would have to initiate removal by submitting a written declaration to Congress. Team Trump likely agrees that Trump’s disappearance from the political scene would improve Republicans’ chances of retaining the White House.

With Democrats soon to control the House and Senate, impeachment is possible and conviction unlikely. But Senate Republicans’ fear of losing in 2028 might change that assumption.

So what happens if Vice President JD Vance becomes president? Assuming he then runs for a full term; how would Vance lead the post-Trump era? Would he denigrate or defend the administration in which he played a starring role? Moreover, if necessary, would Vance pardon Trump, as President Gerald Ford pardoned President Richard Nixon, and risk losing his own election in the process?

Speculation aside, Vance is likely to retain his current title. The question of whether he will run for president without Trump’s endorsement will answered by spring 2027. I suspect that if Trump does not endorse him, Vance will announce that he will not run, and he will save face by citing family concerns. Trump could deflect, saying, “Let the people decide.” He may believe that anyone he endorses would lose the general election because they aren’t him.

Yet if Trump does endorse his likely heir, watch Vance turn himself into a political pretzel, defending Trump to win his “third term” as the president hovers over and monitors his campaign.

Meanwhile, Marco Rubio , secretary of State and national security advisor, is backstage, waiting for the Vance-Trump decision to be resolved. He has long dreamed of becoming the first Hispanic president ( see his 2016 campaign ), but he now carries Trump’s baggage. Will Rubio resign in 2027 to pursue his destiny? Would he “go rogue” and tell the world what he really thinks of Trump, as he did in 2016? If Vance bows out, would Trump endorse Rubio, who would then launch his campaign? What would Trump demand in return for an endorsement? Would Rubio even want Trump’s endorsement?

The latter question is relevant after Trump’s controversial Nov. 20 press conference , during which he said, “I can’t speak to America,” and rambled for nearly 90 minutes. Vance and Rubio stood behind the president like wooden puppets, even as Trump (jokingly) denigrated them as potential successors in favor of Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff. Miller’s performance at the podium, with countless lies and exaggerations was music to Trump’s ears.

For now, Vance and Rubio are caught in Trump’s magnetic political force-field, negatively supercharged since the midterms, resulting in a new tight race among Republican primary voters. RealClearPolitics polling averages show Rubio at 35.4 percent support to Vance’s 34 percent.

Furthermore, until the Trump-Rubio-Vance dance is done, less popular Republican presidential primary wannabes — such as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and soon-to-be former Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis — can only make noise.

Turning to the crowded Democratic field, the RealClear polling averages are meaningless this early, before debates start in June . Still, the big news is that Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) has leapt into second place with 15 percent support and is the man to watch .

Ossoff nips at the heels of first-place former Vice President Harris, who has 16.5 percent support. But the losing 2024 presidential nominee is only treading water with name recognition while debating whether to run again .

Summarizing the 2028 race, Trump, the showman, is the opening and closing act. The unpopular yet powerful lame-duck president is declining but remains the daily wild card. By design, he will dominate the next two chaotic years with jaw-dropping headlines , endless wars, bold lies and exaggerations, while shirking responsibility when things go wrong.

As always — just the way he likes it—Trump is a force of nature shaping the political climate , forcing every candidate to react to him.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008 .

articles.body:
Post-Thanksgiving greetings, gentle readers!

I hope you all are enjoying a peaceful day with loved ones, and nothing more serious to contemplate than whether to have a cold turkey sandwich with cranberry sauce or a hot turkey sandwich with gravy. (Both are valid, but just remember: Turkey gravy comes but once a year and canned cranberries are forever.)

I love Thanksgiving not just for its simplicity and homeliness but for its Americanness. Every culture has some form of a day or ritual observance of gratitude. Our species has known for thousands of years that there is no meaningful happiness that isn’t first rooted in the appreciation of the gifts we have already been given. But America’s Thanksgiving, predating our founding as it does, points to a key part of our national identity — the idea that this place is special and to get to be here is a gift not of a sovereign or a state, but of our creator. Our endowment is not in a government but in the natural rights attached to us from birth. The government, Lord hear our prayer, is supposed to exist to preserve them.

So, I’m not going to serve you any microwaved political leftovers today. We’ve just had a gullywasher of an election, and I suppose we’ve all had our fill of my punditry. But I will make a couple of recommendations even beyond the wisdom of warming your gravy in a saucepan and then using that gravy to reheat your turkey before putting it on the bread.

First, we have a cracking good episode of Bill Sammon’s and my weekly politics stream, “ Whole Hog Politics Live .” It comes online at 9 a.m. ET but will be available anytime thereafter for Hill Insider members’ viewing pleasure. We’re joined by Democratic strategy maven James Carville and former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R). Their policy preferences are as different as I suspect their turkey recipes are, but both of them offer insights and outlooks rooted in a deep love of country — whether that comes deep-fried with Cajun spices or oven-roasted on a New England table worthy of Currier and Ives.

Then, this weekend, we’ve got more goodies on “ The Hill Sunday with Chris Stirewalt .”

It’s our annual great books episode where we will talk with authors about new offerings that we think are good reads, might make us better citizens and could help you check that hard-to-buy-for family member off your holiday shopping list:

Audrye Wong and her timely book, “ Subversion and Seduction: China’s Economic Statecraft ,” Shadi Hamid and Matthew Kaemingk on their collaboration “Can Religion Save Democracy? How More Faith–Not Less–Can Heal Our Public Life.” Walter Stahr and his fantastic and much-needed new biography “ William Howard Taft: A Great American Life ,” and legendary sportswriter Peter King brings us his excellent — and at times controversial — book that is part memoir and part history of the making of the modern NFL, “ The Game .”

Catch us Sunday at 10 a.m. ET on NewsNation or check your local listings to find the local affiliate in your area.

We are most certainly thankful for all of your support and encouragement, readers. Now, get serious about your sandwich strategy!

articles.title: From Hollywood mogul to Biden-Harris insiders, Democrats turn to familiar faces to shape their next chapter
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's transition team director previously claimed Zionists were "controlling" U.S. politics, while Tyler Perry co-chairs Georgia's team.
articles.body: On the heels of the blue wave in the 2026 U.S. midterms, incoming Democratic leaders are tapping an eclectic mix of political veterans, business executives and entertainment figures to help shape their transitions into power. From a Hollywood mogul and former Biden administration officials to figures with ties to Republican leaders, the appointments offer an early glimpse into the people Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern — and the experience and connections they hope to bring into their new administrations. Several incoming Democrats are turning to familiar faces from the Biden administration. In New Mexico, Gov.-elect Deb Haaland tapped former Biden presidential speechwriter Felicia Salazar and former Interior Department official Joan Mooney for her transition team, while California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra selected Arsenio Mataka, who previously served as his senior counselor at the Department of Health and Human Services under Biden, to direct policy for his transition team. In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton tapped Elisabeth Hire, a former aide to then-Vice President Biden, as a transition co-chair. Haaland's campaign and Becerra's campaign each did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The transition teams will help incoming leaders prepare to take office, including identifying potential administration officials, shaping policy priorities and laying the groundwork for their first days in power. The selections also offer a window into the experience, relationships and perspectives newly elected Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., tapped Egyptian-American lawyer Brenda Abdelall as the director of his transition team, Politico Playbook first reported in early November. Abdelall previously claimed that Zionists were "controlling" much of U.S. politics, The Washington Free Beacon reported Nov. 6, though Harris' 2024 presidential campaign said at the time that the remarks did not reflect Abdelall's current views. "The Zionists have a strong voice in American politics," Abdelall told the New York Sun during a conference for the American Muslim Council in 2002, the Free Beacon reported. "I would say they're controlling a lot of it." Abdelall previously served as the assistant secretary of partnership and engagement at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. She also directed the Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign's outreach to Arab American voters, Reuters reported. JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital on Nov. 9 that Abdelall "comes to the role of transition director with decades of experience leading teams at the highest levels of politics, including the Biden-Harris administration." "While at the Department of Homeland Security, Brenda worked to implement the nation’s first National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism and frequently spearheaded efforts to counter the rise of hate crimes and violence across the country," Richner added. "The transition team is committed to building a team that reflects the great diversity of Michigan and ensuring that the El-Sayed office serves all communities across the state." El-Sayed is set to assume office on Jan. 3, 2027. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR-ELECT CALLS TRUMP 'UNSERIOUS FOOL' WHILE DEFENDING COMBATIVE POLITICAL STYLE DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Georgia Democratic Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms announced Nov. 6 that filmmaker and actor Tyler Perry would serve as one of 10 co-chairs of her transition team, dubbed "Georgia's Promise," WBAL-TV reported. Perry has long been known for his philanthropic efforts, including supporting underserved communities and charitable causes across Georgia. Bottoms lauded Perry as "an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta," WDSU reported. EX-BIDEN OFFICIAL WINS GEORGIA DEM PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR IN BID TO END PARTY'S LOSING STREAK The news that Perry will serve on Bottoms’ Georgia transition team has sparked some criticism due to the entertainment mogul facing two active lawsuits accusing him of sexual assault and misconduct, allegations his attorneys have denied, Variety reported Nov. 6. Perry has denied all sexual assault and harassment allegations made against him, People reported on March 3. Maxscene, a division of Tyler Perry Studios, did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Bottoms previously was an executive producer on Netflix’s "Miss Governor," a 2025 political comedy sitcom produced by Tyler Perry Studios, per online film database IMDb. Other prominent figures that have been tapped for Bottoms' transition committee include Home Depot co-founder Arthur Blank and former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance Roz Brewer, WBAL-TV reported. Bottoms’ campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Bottoms is set to take office on Jan. 11, 2027. Texas Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson's transition team includes Mark Penley, a former deputy attorney general who reported outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to the FBI, and Erin Epley, who served as lead attorney in Paxton's impeachment, The Houston Chronicle reported Nov. 16. Johnson also tapped Amanda Crawford, a former appointee of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican sheriff from Terrell County, as part of his transition team, according to the Chronicle. Johnson's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley is also turning to the world of professional sports, tapping Alex Lasry, a former senior vice president of the NBA's Milwaukee Bucks, to serve on his transition team, Wisconsin Public Radio reported Nov. 11. Lasry, the son of former Bucks co-owner and billionaire businessman Marc Lasry, helped oversee the franchise's operations during its rise to the 2021 NBA championship and played a key role in developing Milwaukee's Fiserv Forum arena. He also mounted an unsuccessful bid for the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination in 2022. articles.title: What would net-zero by 2050 cost, and what would it buy? We have the numbers.
articles.summary: Earlier this week, the United Nations Climate Summit in Turkey, collapsed without a final agreement after two days of overtime. More than 130 countries as well as a large number of U.S. states have pledged to reach net zero, most by 2050. Yet through two weeks of talks, the most basic question went unasked: what…
articles.body:
Earlier this week, the United Nations Climate Summit in Turkey, collapsed without a final agreement after two days of overtime. More than 130 countries as well as a large number of U.S. states have pledged to reach net zero, most by 2050. Yet through two weeks of talks, the most basic question went unasked: what would net zero by 2050 cost, and how much good would it do? That is odd, because the UN already owns the tools to find out.

So I built NetZeroCostBenefit.com , a website that lets anyone see what the U.S., or any other country or group of countries, would achieve by reaching net zero in 2050, what it would cost, and what the climate benefit would be worth.

None of the inputs are mine: The climate model it employs, known by the acronym MAGICC , is used throughout the U.N.’s own climate reports and can translate any country’s promised emissions cuts into lower temperatures by the year 2100. The costs come from U.N. surveys of economic models, and the damage estimates come from the two most recent syntheses of the economics of warming.

Anyone can check the arithmetic. For its latest report and updates, the climate panel gathered nearly a thousand model estimates of what climate policy costs. Almost none of them get anywhere near to net-zero by 2050, because it is so hard and costly.

Only three models reach net zero starting from today’s actual emissions, rather than assuming cuts that began years ago. They find that global net-zero would cost between 3 percent and 19 percent of global GDP in 2050. That’s because expensive energy throttles growth.

My website uses the middle estimate, of a loss of 7.2 percent of GDP in 2050 against current policies.

The estimation of benefits comes from the two most recent syntheses of the damage from warming — one by one of the most quoted climate economists, Richard Tol , and the other by William Nordhaus , the only climate economist to win the Nobel Prize in economics. Given the warming the U.N. model projects under current policies, climate change will cost the world 1.8 percent to 2.8 percent of its GDP by 2100. That is a real loss, but nowhere near the catastrophes bandied about. It is also a lot less than a 7.2 percent loss of GDP, and a lot further away.

But then there’s the other side of the equation. Net-zero only avoids part of the climate damage projected. Nor does any single country’s effort buy much. If the U.S. reaches net zero by 2050 and stays there while the rest of the world keeps its current policies, the model projects global temperatures in 2100 would be only 0.14 degrees Fahrenheit lower. So nobody would notice the difference in temperature, but Americans would certainly notice the added costs.

In 2045 alone, the model puts the cost at $1.2 trillion. From 2027 to 2100, the cost adds up to $12.7 trillion in today’s money. The global climate benefit adds up to just under $2 trillion. The American sacrifice delivers 15 cents of benefits for every dollar spent.

Some will object that no country should look at its own numbers this way, because if everyone notices large costs but tiny benefits, nothing will get done. But the math doesn’t improve with pooling. As the website shows, each nation ends up doing much less good for the world than what it puts in by adopting the net-zero goal.

Indeed, when you look at the whole world, global net zero by 2050 would avoid $24 trillion in climate damage this century but cost $255 trillion — both in today’s dollars. So that’s nine cents on the dollar.

The problem isn’t that countries act alone. It is that the policy itself costs far more than it delivers.

Fossil fuels remain cheap and plentiful, despite price fluctuations. It is little wonder that they still supply more than four-fifths of global energy , or that emissions rose again last year. At the pace of the last half-century, they won’t be gone by 2050 — they will be gone a millennium later, in 2997 .

None of this means that climate change is harmless. It is indeed a real challenge, and the smart fix is to invest more in green-energy research and development, so that clean energy eventually outcompetes fossil fuels and becomes cheaper for everyone. Instead, many politicians continue to insist on expensive, inefficient policies, as if industrial economies could run on sunshine and good intentions.

Net-zero by 2050 is an egregiously bad deal. Across 31 climate summits, delegates have ignored this reality. Now, anyone can run the numbers.

Bjorn Lomborg is President of the Copenhagen Consensus, Visiting Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, and author of “False Alarm” and “Best Things First.”

articles.title: Chamberlain appeased Hitler — Zelensky will not and should not appease Putin
articles.summary: In pandering to Putin, Steve Witkoff is effectively echoing Chamberlain’s assessment of the Sudetenland crisis.
articles.body:
History, they say , doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes. Right now, history is much closer to repeating itself.

Or at least, that appears to be the case regarding administration emissary Steve Witkoff’s endless courtship of Russian president Vladimir Putin. As a former senior White House official in the George H.W. Bush administration put it to me this week, “Witkoff says he trusts Putin. It’s the same thing that Neville Chamberlain said about [Adolf] Hitler.”

Actually, Witkoff has gone further than Chamberlain ever did. The American negotiator praised the Russian mass-murderer as “a humanitarian.” Chamberlain never said anything of the sort — he detested Hitler.

In September 1938, two weeks before he capitulated and signed the Munich agreement allowing Hitler to dismember Czechoslovakia and seize the Sudetenland, the British Prime Minister told his cabinet that Hitler was “a gangster” and added that the Nazi dictator was “the commonest little dog I have ever seen.’” If that were not enough, Chamberlain also described him as “entirely undistinguished. You would never notice him in a crowd and would take him for the house painter he once was.”

Hitler had as little respect for Chamberlain as Putin likely has for Witkoff. The boorish Nazi was not as polite about his counterpart, calling him “the old a——.” In public, Putin has told Witkoff and his fellow negotiator Jared Kushner, “We are comfortable working with you.” That does not necessarily indicate what he thinks of them in private.

It is worth recalling that in his effort to seize the Sudetenland, Hitler turned on the charm, and it certainly swayed the British prime minister. As Chamberlain wrote to his sister: “various people who were with Hitler after my interview [said] that he had been very favorably impressed. … In short I had established a certain confidence, which was my aim, and in spite of the hardness and ruthlessness I thought I saw in his face I got the impression that here was a man who could be relied upon when he had given his word.”

Thinking that he could rely on Hitler’s word did not mean that Chamberlain changed his view of the Nazi’s character, however. He bore no illusions about Hitler being anything other than a thug and certainly not a humanitarian.

In claiming the Sudetenland, Hitler employed the same arguments that Putin would conjure up nearly a century later. Hitler asserted that all he wanted was that part of Czechoslovakia whose population was 50 percent German. He also frequently stated that he sought peace but at the same time wanted to rectify the European security balance, which the Versailles Treaty has rendered unfavorable to Germany.

Putin has argued that Russia must incorporate Ukraine’s four oblasts with Russian-speaking majorities. And, like Hitler, he wishes to reconstruct Europe’s security architecture. He seeks to roll back NATO’s post-1997 expansion, or, at a minimum, ensure that NATO does not station any troops in those states that joined the alliance after that date.

In pandering to Putin, and in laying down a framework for a deal that Zelensky might be expected to accept, Witkoff is effectively echoing Chamberlain’s assessment of the Sudetenland crisis as “a quarrel in a faraway country, between people of whom we know nothing.”

Chamberlain felt that Czechoslovakia, a country created after World War I, simply was not worth fighting for or even supporting. Evidently, the American negotiators share a similar view of Ukraine, a country created as the Cold War ended.

The Czechs were actually militarily powerful. Had they received British and French support, they might well have withstood a German assault , if the Nazis had chosen to attack — which they might not have. Nevertheless, Eduard Benes, the Czech president, recognized that neither of the two major European powers was prepared to support him. He felt that he had no choice but to capitulate to Hitler’s demands.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has a different disposition and faces a different situation. Over five years, he has fought the Russians to a standstill while benefitting from intermittent American support and increasing European assistance. Unlike Benes, he is in no mood to capitulate.

Washington reportedly is pressing Zelensky to reach an agreement to terminate the war by year’s end. To do so, he would have to cede four oblasts to Moscow and possibly four others. Zelensky has no incentive to capitulate to Putin; time could be on his side. Whereas Chamberlain told his Cabinet that “Herr Hitler was telling the truth,” Zelensky has no such illusions about Putin. Instead, he knows that in just weeks the Democrats will control Congress and afford him far more support than he is currently receiving. He is unlikely to cave to the Russians; nor should he.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: Democrats, forget the Voting Rights Act: Fix Rucho
articles.summary: Rucho, not Callais, is why Black political representation is disappearing in some states.
articles.body:
The left has been apoplectic about the gutting of the Voting Rights Act by the conservative majority on the U.S. Supreme Court.

The final nail in the coffin was Louisiana v. Callais this past term, which held that a violation of the Voting Rights Act requires intentional racial discrimination and further prohibited the intentional creation of Black congressional districts without such a showing. The court also observed that gerrymanders with political motivations are not necessarily racially discriminatory, even if they negatively affect Black voters.

But this justifiable concern with the Voting Rights Act is obscuring a greater immediate threat. What really undermines Black political representation in America is not Callais, but a 2019 case on a different subject: Rucho v. Common Cause , which held that political gerrymanders cannot be challenged in federal court no matter how extreme. Partisan gerrymanders were held by the court to be political questions. Rucho, not Callais, is why Black political representation is disappearing in some states.

To understand the interplay of Callais and Rucho, one need only look at what happened in Tennessee. Memphis used to have an urban core of Black voters in one compact congressional district next to a large, white-dominated suburban and rural district. That older map, adopted in 2022, reflected the normal pattern of legislative districting based on how Americans tend to group themselves.

Once Callais was decided, however, the Tennessee state legislature removed the longstanding ban on mid-decade congressional redistricting and carved Memphis up into three sprawling congressional districts , two of which extended all the way to Nashville, 200 miles away.

The resulting congressional map pays no attention to traditional districting norms, such as compactness and preservation of political boundaries. It looks more like a plate of spaghetti than a congressional district map. The result was three white districts and no Black district.

All this was clearly intentional. You would think that it obviously violates Callais’s ban on intentional racial discrimination. But it probably does not, because of Callais’s strong suggestion that political gerrymanders are not necessarily racially discriminatory even when Black voters lose out.

The Republicans in the Tennessee legislature freely admitted that they were redistricting to eliminate a likely Democratic congressional district in Memphis. Hence, this was a political, not a racial, gerrymander. Black voters were just collateral damage. Under Callais, this is not a violation of the Voting Rights Act.

Forget that this reasoning is absurd, as if political partisans could not also be racist. The point is that Congress can act to undo what happened to Memphis.

Congress cannot directly reverse Callais. The Supreme Court was interpreting the Voting Rights Act against a background of equal protection principles. If Congress tried to weaken the intentional discrimination standard, the conservative majority on the court would very likely find the effort unconstitutional.

What Congress can do is reverse Rucho. In that case, the court held that political gerrymanders represent a political question because it is not obvious what a fair legislative map looks like. There was no judicially manageable standard.

But a judicial judgment like that is subject to change by Congress, which has wide discretion to enforce voting standards for congressional elections. All Congress has to do is ban congressional maps in which partisan considerations substantially predominate over traditional districting norms. Congress could even go further and prohibit mid-decade redistricting and weirdly shaped maps altogether.

With these changes, Tennessee’s treatment of Memphis would be plainly illegal. Memphis would very likely be restored to its simple, compact congressional district.

Admittedly, a federal statute like that would not really increase Black representation. It would only outlaw the worst Republican excesses. Many people would like to see a more aggressive challenge to the court’s voting rights interpretations.

That fight, however, is not likely to be successful, at least in the short run. For now, Congress should act to keep Republicans from eliminating Black representation everywhere they have a state legislative majority. A simple federal statute outlawing excessive political gerrymanders would do that without the likelihood of a prolonged legal challenge.

Democrats overcame a lot of the Republican gerrymandering in the 2026 midterm elections But even with the blue tsunami, the Republican gerrymander of Memphis worked. Three white Republicans were elected . And in future elections, the existing Republican gerrymanders are going to be more effective than they were in 2026, with its lopsided Democratic majorities.

If Democrats want to retain control of the House in the future, overturning Rucho is absolutely necessary. And, fortunately, it would not be hard to do.

Returning the Voting Rights Act to its rightful place as promoting an increase in Black political participation is a worthy goal. But that goal cannot become an excuse for not acting to protect Black voters immediately. Democrats should forget about the Voting Rights Act for now and overturn Rucho first.

Bruce Ledewitz is a professor of law emeritus at the Thomas R. Kline School of Law of Duquesne University. He is the author of the forthcoming book, “The Last Master of the Tradition: Charles Black and the Future of Constitutional Democracy.”

images.caption: Voting rights activists gather outside the Supreme Court in Washington, early Wednesday, Oct. 15, 2025, as the justices prepare to take up a major Republican-led challenge to the Voting Rights Act, the centerpiece legislation of the Civil Rights Movement. (AP Photo/Cliff Owen)

articles.title: ‘Playing with fire’: Trump faces GOP backlash over Nvidia CEO’s return
articles.summary: Former Trump officials warn his push to reinstate NVIDIA’s CEO could be the final straw for Republicans.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in getting NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang reinstated has drawn little support from his own party with some Republican officials warning this could be a blow to the president’s popularity with his conservative base.

Earlier this week, the US president ignited a firestorm across Washington, DC, after he revealed he personally contacted NVIDIA’s board of directors and “convinced” its members to let Huang return.

Trump said he spoke to the board “directly and indirectly” in the less than two weeks between Huang’s resignation and his reinstatement, amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The move amounted to an extraordinary intervention by the US president, whose predecessors, both Democratic and Republican, have largely avoided personally involving themselves – or their administrations – in corporate matters.

“I felt very strongly about it,” Trump told CNBC on Monday about his decision to contact NVIDIA’s board. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the … company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.”

After Huang’s resignation , shares of NVIDIA, which financial disclosures show Trump holds tens of millions of dollars of stock in, dropped sharply, wiping out more than $1tn in market value. They rebounded after Huang was reinstated.

A White House spokesperson told Al Jazeera that “Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and neither Trump nor any of his family members has input on how investments are made.

Several Republican lawmakers in the US Senate have publicly objected to Huang’s reinstatement , expressing alarm that China, via the tech executive’s affair, may have obtained access to NVIDIA’s chips for its artificial intelligence arms race against the US. They have not, however, mentioned Trump’s foray into the matter.

“The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” Republican Senator Tom Cotton, a member of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China and the Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, posted to social media. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip-export control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”

US Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead Republicans in the chamber when they enter the minority at the start of the next Congress in January, told Al Jazeera in a statement that Huang’s actions create “a significant national security vulnerability”.

“Through vigorous oversight and adoption of strong, bipartisan export-control measures, Congress will do its part to ensure our national security interests are being met,” Thune said. “The American people expect and deserve no less.”

Trump said NVIDIA’s board sought assurances that Huang did not pose a national security risk because of his relationship with Alice Huang, the former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials suspect of working for China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has denied the allegation.

The US president, who said the NVIDIA CEO had been “exonerated”, noted that his assessment aligned with one conducted by the US Department of Justice. But in a news conference on Tuesday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche sidestepped questions about a reported investigation into Huang.

Privately, several former US Republican officials have told Al Jazeera it could be the final straw after a decade with a leader that some in the GOP have said has never been bound by traditional conservative principles.

“How very President Xi of him,” a former Trump administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak candidly, said of the US president’s “communist-esque” actions in getting involved with NVIDIA, likening them to ones taken by the Chinese leader. “I think that sets a dangerous precedent.”

The official, who worked with Trump in the White House during his first term, described the modern-day US Republican Party as a tripod supported by three key values: religion, free market economics and national security.

But after Trump said he intervened with NVIDIA’s board to get Huang back on top, a leg of the “conservative stool,” they said, was broken.

“You need all three to stand. And he just ripped one out,” the official said. “So, at some point, the chair falls.”

“If he’s going to betray national security … why wouldn’t he betray the other legs, you know, on social conservative and economic issues?” they added. “I think it raises a lot of questions for folks and … he’s playing with fire.”

Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist who serves on several corporate boards, said NVIDIA, not Trump, will bear responsibility for reinstating Huang.

“If the president wants to make a phone call, because he’s concerned about chips or concerned about the macroeconomics of the impact of NVIDIA failing, that’s his prerogative,” Davis said. “It’s whether NVIDIA’s board wants to vote that way or not, and they did.”

Next week, Huang is slated to participate in a transcribed interview with the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, as well as a separate public hearing with the Senate Banking Committee.

One of the latter’s Republican members, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, said he expects Huang will “take the Fifth Amendment so he doesn’t incriminate himself in criminal prosecution.”

“It’s not my place as a senator to tell Mr Huang that he can’t cheat on his wife,” Kennedy told Fox News on Tuesday. “It is my place to tell him if you’re cheating on your wife with somebody who could be a Chinese spy, that jeopardises national security.”

A separate former Trump administration official who also spoke on condition of anonymity to speak openly about the situation told Al Jazeera the hearings would be “awful” for the US president – and they might even lead to significant political ramifications for him.

“If they are as bad as I think they will be, you could see Republicans talking about impeachment”, they said.

But some doubt this will be Trump’s undoing, noting that he has bounced back before from actions that crossed red lines for many Republicans.

“We’ve asked ourselves that same question for 10 years: ‘Is this what will cause Republicans to speak out against Trump?” Doug Heye, a former director of communications for the Republican National Committee, said. “Who knows at this point?”

articles.title: America deserves answers and accountability for the measles outbreak
articles.summary: We need to understand how we ended up in this growing American tragedy, for which losing vaccine elimination status is a harbinger of worse to come.
articles.body:
On Nov. 13, amid news of a massive communication failure in the federal air traffic control system, the U.S. lost measles elimination status with the Pan American Health Organization.

Public and federal officials are already clamoring for accountability for the massive air traffic disruption. Yet there is little call for federal accountability as we endure a major breach in community protection, resulting in exploding measles cases across the U.S. and the loss of elimination status.

The anti-vaccine movement in the U.S. has been growing for years, kindled over the past several decades by a fraudulent report claiming a link between autism and the measles vaccine. Despite the retraction of the report and abundant evidence showing no link between vaccines and autism , this notion has been perpetuated.

Measles is so contagious that 95 percent of the public needs to be vaccinated to stop its spread in the U.S. Since 2000, measles outbreaks in the U.S. have largely been attributed to international introduction. This is no longer the case, as measles is now spreading in communities in more than 40 states . Studies also show that a drop in U.S. vaccination rates to 90 percent may result in 11 million cases over the next two decades, with an economic impact in billions of dollars.

The COVID-19 pandemic was the moment the anti-vaccine movement had been waiting for. The COVID-19 vaccine was developed under the Trump administration and released in December 2020. When the Biden administration began, it initiated protocols for the broad distribution of the vaccines.

Following a very contentious election, Republicans opposed COVID-19 policies proposed by the Biden administration, including vaccine mandates. Thus, after initial nationwide enthusiasm for COVID vaccination, the vaccine became politicized. Over the second 18 months of the pandemic, one of the biggest risk factors for dying from COVID-19 was who you voted for, with deaths of unvaccinated Republicans outstripping those of vaccinated Democrats, a concept referred to as “ Red COVID “.

Not long after, Republicans began welcoming the anti-vaccine movement with rallying cries of “ personal freedom ” and “ my body, my choice .” Yet these calls are a Trojan horse, part of the anti-vaccine agenda that resonates with conservative groups better than the claim that vaccines cause autism. Anti-COVID-control efforts also turned against medical expertise , with politicians attacking medical and public health experts.

Midway through the pandemic, opposition to COVID-19 vaccines spilled over into routine childhood immunizations. Nationally, we began to see legislation drafted against public health and childhood vaccination .

During the 2024 presidential election primaries, Robert Kennedy Jr., a trial lawyer with anti-vaccine views who received millions of dollars from the anti-vaccine movement, developed a following linked to the Make America Healthy Again movement. Eager for Kennedy-followers’ votes, President Trump pledged an administration in return for his support. Thus, an individual with anti-vaccine views and without a background in medicine became secretary of Health and Human Services .

When the first major outbreak of measles in decades took place in 2024 in Texas, rather than invoking standard public health measures to curtail it, Kennedy did not advocate for vaccination but instead called for vitamin treatment.

Not long after, parents, left on their own and confused about the merits of measles vaccines, began to increasingly use religious and/or personal vaccine exemptions to opt out, and national childhood vaccination rates fell. Some states also made it easier to claim exemptions or prohibited anti-exemption policies.

While the invisible shield of public health that protects us from contagious diseases has been breached by the Trump administration, Republicans and Democrats overwhelmingly support requiring a standard series of vaccines for children to enter school. Yet a small proportion of unvaccinated people is enough to put our communities at risk of serious vaccine-preventable illnesses, justifying vaccine requirements.

During this month’s blue wave election , the Trump administration and Republicans were held accountable for policies that led to surging inflation and soaring fuel prices. After thousands of flights were disrupted due to failures in the Federal Aviation Administration’s communication platform, Congress will soon seek accountability .

However, the flight disruptions did not result in thousands of people becoming ill , hundreds of hospitalizations, congenital infections or deaths, as is happening now with measles. We need to understand how we ended up in this growing American tragedy, for which losing vaccine elimination status is a harbinger of worse to come.

Dr. Scott A. Rivkees is a pediatrician. He is the former state surgeon general and secretary of Health of Florida.

articles.title: 5 big questions for Democrats this Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Democrats are entering the last month of the year on a high. The midterm election results surpassed all but the most optimistic expectations for the party. Even six months ago, the idea of the Democrats racking up a net gain of nine seats in the Senate would have seemed implausible. Their final House majority will…
articles.body:
Democrats are entering the last month of the year on a high.

The midterm election results surpassed all but the most optimistic expectations for the party. Even six months ago, the idea of the Democrats racking up a net gain of nine seats in the Senate would have seemed implausible. Their final House majority will have a margin of greater than 80 seats.

The outcome has given the opposition party the leverage to investigate President Trump’s actions and to constrain any new legislative moves that he might make.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

At the same time, Democrats face challenges of their own, including how to navigate internal tensions and how to best prioritize their next moves.

Here are five questions facing the Democratic Party this Thanksgiving.

Can they get stuff done on affordability?

The Democratic victory in the midterms was fueled in significant part by voter discontent over the cost of living — and a perception that Trump and the GOP had failed to address the problem.

Now the onus will be on Democrats to take action and show progress.

Soon-to-be-Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) outlined in a recent interview with Lulu Garcia-Navarro of The New York Times how his party might go about this.

Jeffries said Democrats would seek to revoke the massive cuts to Medicaid and to SNAP benefits that were part of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The GOP legislation is projected to cut around $1 trillion f rom Medicaid and around $186 billion from SNAP over the next decade.

Jeffries also suggested Democrats would seek to roll back the Trump tariffs that many economists believe have added to inflationary pressures, even as the president insists otherwise.

A larger unknown is what will happen with the war on Iran, which has caused energy prices to rise. Democrats could try to force an end to the conflict, perhaps trying to choke off funding. But Trump remains as unpredictable as ever on the topic.

There is another political question on affordability, too. If public perception in 12 or 18 months is that the cost of living remains unacceptably high, how will blame be doled out among the Democrats and Trump?

How will they manage tensions between the left and center-left?

Before the midterms triumph, Democrats had a rather fraught primary season, with challengers on the progressive left facing off against more establishment-friendly, centrist rivals.

The left did not prevail everywhere, but it saw some big victories. Most prominently, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) vanquished Rep. Haley Stevens (D) in the primary before defeating former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in the general election.

There were other examples, too, including primary victories over Democratic incumbents for leftist figures such as Melat Kiros in Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York. Kiros and Chevalier, both of whom easily won their general election races, are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

The progressive candidates capitalized in part on a sense among parts of the Democratic base that party leadership has been too timid in fighting back against Trump and is too unambitious in its policy prescriptions. The issue of Israel and Palestine is also a visceral one.

Even so, numerous centrist officeholders are wary of the progressives, fearing that the left’s ideas have less appeal in electoral battlegrounds than among primary voters.

The internal debates aren’t about to end anytime soon. They could burn even hotter once Democrats take the reins of power on Capitol Hill.

The left-vs.-center tensions will infuse the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 as well.

A number of significant figures are publicly contemplating running. None has yet made an official declaration, but someone will fire the starting pistol soon enough.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is seen by most as almost certain to run. Less clear is whether 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris will try again, or whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) will enter the fray.

A potential Ocasio-Cortez run is especially intriguing because, if she goes for it, she is likely to be the undisputed standard-bearer of the left. If Ocasio-Cortez passes on a bid, several other candidates could seek the progressive mantle.

The centrist faction in the party will get representation in the presidential field too, especially if the likes of Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear or former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel run.

How does Van Hollen do in his challenge to Schumer?

This is the question of the moment inside the Beltway.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is accruing at least some support as he seeks to defeat the long-standing Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as the party prepares to take the majority in the upper chamber.

Van Hollen is just nine years younger than the 76-year-old Schumer and hardly a hard-left figure. But he is positioning himself as the option for those who want more progressive leadership — including on the Israel-Palestine question — or who are pressing for generational change.

The Maryland senator has received public support from progressives including El-Sayed, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Sen-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) and, on Wednesday , Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

But not all his backers are in the left-wing camp. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) is also among Van Hollen’s supporters.

Schumer remains the favorite to win the leadership contest, and his loyalists question why the party would throw him overboard after such a successful election cycle.

Still, the final vote will be an important barometer of satisfaction, or dissatisfaction, with Schumer and with party leadership more generally.

Incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) had a message for Republicans as the results rolled in on Election Night: “Lawyer up,” he wrote on social media .

It’s clear that Democrats will launch several investigations into the Trump administration. Their base will not settle for anything less, especially given the sheer numbers and scale of Trump-related controversies.

At the same time, some strategists worry that a focus on Trump is not necessarily the most effective gambit as the party seeks to consolidate its 2026 victories and win the White House in 2028.

Others argue it is perfectly feasible for Democrats to take a twin-track approach, seeking both to hold Trump and his allies accountable while advancing policies on kitchen-table issues.

articles.title: Votar ebrio en España es posible y ya hay precedentes: el presidente de la mesa electoral tiene potestad para expulsar a cualquiera del colegio electoral
articles.standfirst: En nuestro país se ha alterado el orden en varias ocasiones por los efectos del alcohol
articles.summary: En nuestro país se ha alterado el orden en varias ocasiones por los efectos del alcohol
articles.body: Este próximo domingo, 29 de noviembre (29N) tendrán lugar las elecciones generales en nuestro país. Los ciudadanos están llamados a las urnas para decidir si optan por un cambio de Gobierno o si prefieren seguir con el actual. Sin embargo, hay una pregunta que se suelen hacer algunos internautas: ¿qué sucede si acudo a votar en estado ebrio? Pues bien, desde la cuenta de YouTube @alminuto3d, recogieron lo que dice la ley al respecto y pidieron tener “mucho ojo”, ya que la respuesta final de la normativa “sorprende”. En concreto, todo aparece regulado en la Ley Orgánica 5/1985, de 19 de junio, del Régimen Electoral General (LOREG), aunque no hay ninguna referencia ni estipulación directa en lo que respecta al alcohol. Desde la citada cuenta indicaron que la ley anteriormente mencionada no dice nada del alcohol, tal y como hemos mencionado: “No hay control de alcoholemia, ni soplar, ni análisis”, ironizaron al respecto. Sin embargo, la legislación electoral sí que refleja en su artículo 91.1 que el presidente de la mesa electoral tiene la autoridad exclusiva para mantener el orden, asegurar la libertad de los electores y garantizar el cumplimiento de la ley. Por lo que si se altera el orden y se monta un espectáculo derivado de un estado de embriaguez, este intervendrá y si no, podría solicitar ayuda a las fuerzas policiales, según aparece estipulado en el artículo 92. Si sucede cualquier incidente que afecte al orden en el colegio electoral deberá reflejado en el acta de la sesión (artículo 94). De esta manera, el citado usuario recalcó que hay que tener “mucho ojo”. Además, pusieron dos ejemplos recientes. En 2019, en Valencia, un hombre ebrio votó en una mesa que no era la suya, metiendo dos papeletas en cada urna. Tuvieron que parar la votación y el caso acabó en el juzgado de guardia. Además, ese mismo año, en Tarragona, el presidente de una mesa llegó borracho y lo acabaron sustituyendo por el suplente.

articles.title: Portnoy says Vance ‘done’ as 2028 presidential contender
articles.summary: Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy, who has used his large social media following to promote President Trump, said Vice President Vance has no chance of winning the White House in 2028. During an interview on “The Scott Jennings Show” on Tuesday, Portnoy told the conservative commentator that he favored Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) as…
articles.body:
Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy, who has used his large social media following to promote President Trump, said Vice President Vance has no chance of winning the White House in 2028.

During an interview on “The Scott Jennings Show” on Tuesday, Portnoy told the conservative commentator that he favored Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) as the GOP nominee.

“I like the way he’s run Florida. Like, I’m here, it’s the only state that turned red, stayed red, barely, and I think he’s pretty good,” Portnoy said, after Jennings asked if he preferred Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
