“I would go Rubio over — I think this: I think JD’s done. Like, I don’t think he has a chance. I think he’s too closely affiliated with Trump,” Portnoy said.

“And I also, I don’t know how you go — he’s going to have to distance himself from Trump, and I don’t know how you go from ‘Trump was the worst’ to ‘Trump was the best’ back to ‘Trump was not so good,’ which he would have to do to win,” he added.

The GOP faced a walloping in this year’s midterms, with the Democrats taking back the House and Senate, even winning in places where the party has historically struggled, like Texas and Kansas.

Trump’s approval rating was at record lows ahead of Election Day and was sitting at 35.80 percent on Friday morning, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, with his disapproval rating at 61.6 percent.

Talk of a potential Rubio bid in 2028 has recently heated up, while enthusiasm for Vance has cooled in the wake of the midterms.

Vance emerged from the midterms blaming the Iran war for the GOP drubbing, and he declined to say whether he supported Trump’s decision to launch the war when asked last week.

The headwinds facing any Republican nominee in 2028 have spurred speculation that Vance may wait out the upcoming election.

Portnoy spoke to NPR in July about his new book, noting the “manosphere” had largely turned on Trump over the Iran war.

He told NPR last year that his support for Trump in 2024 was more “an indictment of the Democrats than an endorsement of Trump’s politics.”

He also said he had a less hard-line view on immigration.

“I don’t necessarily think you should go back in time,” he told NPR. “If somebody isn’t here legally, but they’re a productive member of society with no issues, I don’t think that you go say, ‘Get out of here.'”

Trump hasn’t backed a successor, suggesting last week that chief of staff Stephen Miller could make a good president.

DeSantis is among a handful of governors seen as potential 2028 contenders, along with outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia and former Gov. Glenn Youngkin of Virginia. Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) is also seen as a likely candidate.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: 14 years of DACA isn’t a milestone — it’s a failure of Congress
articles.summary: This isn’t a policy debate anymore. It’s machinery of government breaking down in real time, and hundreds of thousands of people are caught in the gears.
articles.body:
Fourteen years ago, the Department of Homeland Security established the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals or DACA program. It was designed to provide, temporarily, hundreds of thousands of young immigrants who were raised, educated and deeply rooted in the U.S. with protection from deportation, and to give them the ability to work legally. It was never meant to be a permanent solution, but a stopgap measure taken via executive action in the face of congressional inaction.

Today, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is failing these hundreds of thousands of young people, as renewals stall and Congress continues to put off action.

Every DACA holder must renew his or her status every two years to keep working legally. If that renewal isn’t processed on time, employers must let the workers go as soon as their permits lapse. DACA recipients, who are required to have been in the country since at least June 15, 2007, lose protection at that point from deportation.

The delays have gotten measurably worse in the past year. DACA renewal applications, which took an average of two weeks to process in fiscal 2025, now take four to six months, with one in five recipients waiting more than seven months. Citizenship and Immigration Services has completed roughly 40 percent fewer renewals in fiscal 2026 than it had at this point in 2025.

This isn’t a policy debate anymore. It’s machinery of government breaking down in real time, and hundreds of thousands of people are caught in the gears.

Because of the increasing delays, the DACA population has shrunk by roughly 100,000 people since January 2025, falling from 533,000 at the beginning of 2025 to 436,000 in June 2026. These individuals are falling out of status through no fault of their own. They are stuck waiting on paperwork.

A program that exists to keep people in the workforce is now doing the opposite: stripping status from people through procedural delays. Employers can lose trained staff with no warning; families lose income overnight. People who are here legally can be deported without warning. None of this reflects any change in eligibility or any new finding about a person’s record, but an agency that cannot keep pace with its own caseload.

The current administration, once threatening to end the program entirely, notably has not done so ; one has to wonder whether these delays are a means to end the program by attrition. Regardless, legislation would end the instability for good.

This group of people has been vetted more than any other group of immigrants in the United States. Every one of them has already been fingerprinted, background-checked and re-vetted every two years since the program began. Nearly 90 percent of all DACA recipients are employed , paying taxes and building lives in the only country most of them remember. If the renewal issues persist, the American workforce will lose tens of thousands of skilled workers. Moreover, most of them have families, and yet are limited in how much they can really contribute to the country by the very temporariness of their status.

Both Republicans and Democrats, including President Trump , have called on Congress to create a permanent solution for these people. It’s time for them to put their votes where their statements are and pass the DREAM Act, or any of several other pieces of bipartisan legislation that have been proposed over the last 20 years.

Fourteen years of the DACA program isn’t a milestone to be celebrated. It’s evidence of a failure of Congress to act on an issue they have said they want to fix. Maybe it’s just one of many areas they have failed to act upon, but this one has human consequences.

Theresa Cardinal Brown has worked for more than 30 years in immigration law, policy and practice. She served in policy roles at U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, and is currently a fellow at the National Immigration Forum and a leader in the Council on National Security and Immigration.

images.caption: LOS ANGELES, CA – SEPTEMBER 10: Frances Yasmeen Motiwalla passes the tents of homeless people at an encampment in an underpass as thousands of immigrants and supporters join the Defend DACA March to oppose the President Trump order to end DACA on September 10, 2017 in Los Angeles, California. The Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program provides undocumented people who arrived to the US as children temporary legal immigration status for protection from deportation to a country many have not known, and a work permit for a renewable two-year period. The order exposes about 800,000 so-called ÒdreamersÓ who signed up for DACA to deportation. About a quarter of them live in California. Congress has the option to replace the policy with legislation before DACA expires on March 5, 2018. (Photo by David McNew/Getty Images)

Progressive media personality Cenk Uygur on Thursday backed Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) as a candidate in the 2028 presidential race if he decides to run.

I’m a left-wing populist, so it makes sense,” Uygur said on a Twitch stream of his nephew Hasan Piker, another notable left-wing personality.

“He’s already proven himself. Got the Epstein files released. Showed incredible — both bravery and action and leadership. Is the most in favor of ending this [Iran] war. He’s for zeroing out aid to Israel. He’s called [Israel’s actions in the Gaza war] a genocide. I think those are litmus tests. We can come back to those issues. And, you know, most importantly, he’s going to win,” he added.

Politico was the first to report on the endorsement from Uygur .

Earlier this month , allies of Khanna launched an effort to press him to run for the White House.

Heading up the “Run Ro” draft committee are former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and progressive political activist Nomiki Konst, per a news release shared with The Hill’s partner network NewsNation.

The committee also features members of former President Obama’s and Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) presidential campaigns.

Khanna has not officially announced a bid for the White House, though he has publicly weighed a bid.

The Hill has reached out to Khanna’s office for comment.

The California Democrat has been in the political spotlight in the past two years, co-leading an effort alongside Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to release files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The 2028 Democratic presidential primary is expected to be a crowded one, particularly in the wake of this month’s sweeping midterm election victories for the party.

articles.title: Keep the filibuster, but make senators earn it
articles.summary: The author proposes reforming the Senate filibuster by requiring a talking component and flipping the burden of proof to ensure legislative accountability.
articles.body:
Ask most Americans what a filibuster looks like and they will describe Jimmy Stewart in “ Mr. Smith Goes to Washington ”: a lone senator on his feet, hoarse and unshaven, refusing to yield the floor until the nation has heard him out. It is a good image. It is also fiction, and not only because it is a movie.

Until the early 1970s , senators who wanted to stop a bill had to hold the floor and talk. Today a senator need only send an email to the majority leader threatening a filibuster. That tells the leader the Senate will need 60 votes before it can even begin to discuss the bill. In practice, the bill never reaches the floor, no one has to explain why, and the public never learns who put on the brakes.

The world’s greatest deliberative body has ground to a halt, which is why calls to abolish the filibuster now come from all sides. President Trump wants it gone. So do several newly elected Democratic senators, among them Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and James Talarico (D-Texas ).

But abolition gets the diagnosis wrong. The problem is not that the Senate protects unlimited debate. The problem is that the Senate no longer requires any debate. The minority can block legislation without accountability. It should earn that right on the floor, not from behind a computer screen.

Accountability runs in both directions. A majority should not be able to silence the minority with a timer, and a minority should not be able to stop the majority from governing with an email.

To get there, two fixes are needed. The first is the talking filibuster, which Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) has advocated for more than a decade: if you want to block a vote, you hold the floor. You may take turns. You may speak for weeks. But you must talk.

The second is the burden of proof. Today the majority must produce 60 votes to move forward, while the minority produces nothing. The solution, which the political scientist Norman Ornstein has long urged , is to flip it: the opponents should show they have the votes to keep debating. If they cannot, debate ends, and a majority vote follows.

Together, these two fixes mean the 41 senators who can now suffocate a bill from their offices would have to come to the floor, make their case, and be counted, again and again. The moment they stopped doing either, the Senate would vote.

Consider the kill switch at work on the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act in 2024. In January it passed the House 357-70. On Aug. 1, a motion to take it up drew 48 votes in favor and 44 against , a majority. It died without discussion. The senators who blocked it were back in their offices within the hour. That is not democracy.

To be sure, a determined minority could still hold the floor for a long time, and the majority would have to keep the Senate in session to outlast it. That is a real cost. It is also the point. Obstruction should reflect conviction, not convenience. And most of these fights would end not in exhaustion but in negotiation, because a stalemate the public can watch costs both sides. The silent filibuster makes compromise unnecessary. The talking filibuster makes it attractive.

The usual objection is that Senate rules can be changed only by a two-thirds vote that a divided chamber will never produce. Yet in 2013, a Democratic majority established by simple majority that most nominations could no longer be filibustered. In 2017, a Republican majority extended that to the Supreme Court. Each was done by a point of order sustained by 51 senators, and each is now settled practice. A talking filibuster could be adopted the same way.

It is understandable that freshman senators will be tempted to end the filibuster. It stands in the way of what they promised to do. But someday, they or their successors will be in the minority and will want a way to make the majority listen.

A new Congress will be seated in January, when the rules can be reset. The question I would put to every senator is this: Would you accept this reformed filibuster from your opponents when your party is in the minority? If so, support it now, while the question is still about the institution rather than the next vote.

Mr. Smith had it right. Let the senators talk. Let the minority make its case. Let it earn its delay. But if they stop talking, let the Senate vote.

John P. Giraudo is a lawyer and a Henry Crown Fellow of the Aspen Institute.

(AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

articles.title: Mamdani's top 4 socialist promises met with reality checks as his first year in office nears its end
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze covers only about 1 million rent-stabilized units, while his city-run grocery pilot faces long lines and shortages.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a socialist, has begun delivering on several of his signature campaign promises in his first year leading the largest city in the U.S. But the limited scope of those efforts raises questions about how much of his far-left agenda he can realistically implement. Fox News Digital breaks down some of Mamdani's most controversial campaign promises and those he's made a priority in the first of his four years in office. NYC MAYOR TOUTS ‘SOCIALIST’ WINS IN FIRST 100 DAYS ALONGSIDE BERNIE SANDERS Rent freezes On the campaign trail, Mamdani pitched freezing monthly rent costs as a key strategy to lower the cost of housing for New Yorkers. Roughly 67.7% of those who live in the five boroughs of the city are renters, according to the most recent government data released in 2024. "As mayor, I will freeze the rent every year that I’m in office. That’s a guarantee," Mamdani said in a campaign video posted near the beginning of his campaign in 2024. True to his word, the New York City Rent Guidelines Board announced Mamdani’s promised freeze in June, detailing a 0% increase in one-year leases beginning between October 2026 and October 2027 and a 0% increase for two-year leases beginning in the same window. Mamdani hailed the announcement as a significant victory for the city, highlighting the longer-lease lock. "This is a historic victory for New York City tenants. After reviewing the data and hearing from New Yorkers across the city, the independent RGB has delivered a freeze on one-year leases, and the first-ever freeze on two-year leases in our city’s history," Mamdani’s office said in a press release in June. "This is the relief that working people across our city deserve." Notably, the freeze does not apply to all rental apartments in New York City, instead covering about 1 million rent-stabilized units. According to the Community Service Society, a nonprofit poverty advocacy group, rent-stabilized apartments make up 41% of the city’s rental units. City-run grocery stores Although Mamdani’s city-run grocery stores haven’t yet launched in earnest, a pilot test of what they could look like has raised questions about whether the idea will meaningfully address the food scarcity issues Mamdani highlighted on the campaign trail. "This month we got polling that showed that two-thirds of New Yorkers support city-owned grocery stores, a policy we’ve championed for months and would guarantee cheaper groceries," Mamdani said last year. Even so, the first version of the city-run grocery store was met with complaints of long lines, shortages and disorganization when it launched in February. MAMDANI’S AFFORDABILITY REVOLUTION STUMBLED AS RENT COSTS SOAR TO RECORD HIGHS In a recent interview, Mamdani said he still has plans to build on the idea. "What we’re going to do is — in a city of more than a thousand supermarkets — we’re going to create five. … They’re cheaper supermarkets, supermarkets with a discount," the mayor said during a recent interview with The New York Times. Mamdani has said he hopes to sell products at 30% below the market price. The proposal has sparked skepticism from economists and commentators over how the city could deliver such steep discounts in an industry known for razor-thin profit margins. With grocery prices up about 33% nationwide since 2019, critics say the plan must explain how prices could undercut private retailers by 30% without significant public subsidies. "This is completely insane. Also, not possible unless taxpayers are subsidizing all the groceries. Grocery store profits are tiny, a few percentage points a year, at best," Outkick founder Clay Travis wrote. Universal childcare Like his grocery store initiative, Mamdani’s plan to implement free universal childcare has struggled to keep pace with demand, falling short of the full promise. "Since the beginning of this campaign, I’ve championed universal childcare, making a commitment to deliver it to New Yorkers as young as six weeks to five years of age," Mamdani said in a campaign video in 2025. Mamdani argued that, without expanded childcare, the city would experience billions in lost productivity from workers who couldn’t enter the workforce. "My administration will address this crisis by providing no-cost childcare to families with children as young as six weeks up until they’re five years of age." STEVE FORBES: MAMDANI’S SOCIALIST RENT-CONTROL PUTS NEW YORK ON THE ROAD TO HOUSING RUIN To facilitate the plan, Mamdani said he believed using government spaces, co-locating with the Department of Education, subsidizing commercial rent and relaxing regulatory requirements would help bring down costs. Mamdani launched his plans back in January, announcing a preliminary version of the plan. The rollout was limited to select areas in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens and only applied to 2-year-old children. In an August press release, Mamdani said the program had a 2,000-seat capacity and over 5,700 applicants, leaving roughly 3,700 children on waitlists. In the same release, Mamdani said he expected the city’s capacity to grow sixfold, going from 2,000 to 12,000. The New York City Independent Budget Office, a government watchdog, confirmed the program’s $73 million cost and estimated that the expanded version would cost roughly $425 million in 2028. According to the United States Census, there are approximately 489,000 children in New York City under the age of 5. Fare-free buses Mamdani’s free bus plans have put him at odds with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul over whether the state should shoulder more of the burden for the mayor’s designs, leaving his campaign promises only partially fulfilled amid costs that would exceed his initial estimations. Early on in his administration, Mamdani was asked when New Yorkers could expect the promise of free fares. Mamdani left the answer open-ended but pledged to fulfill his commitment by the end of his term. "I have said when we ran this campaign … I’m making buses fast and free. I have said that by the time I am done being mayor, those will have been delivered," Mamdani said in January. So far, Mamdani has taken steps toward increasing busing efficiency in NYC by developing 50 priority corridors for speed improvements. But discussions about making the buses free have stalled at the state level. New York’s bus system is run through the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), a state-created public authority. The body is controlled by the governor, who appoints the MTA chair and its board. The group makes controlling decisions about its fares. Although she expressed sympathy toward Mamdani’s design, Hochul said she could not remove the sources of revenue from New York City’s public transportation. "I cannot set forth a plan right now that takes money out of a system that relies on the fares of the buses and the subways. But can we find a path to make it more affordable for people who need help? Of course we can," Hochul said at a political retreat earlier this year. Mamdani’s campaign originally estimated the plan would come with a $700 million price tag. However, the New York City Independent Budget Office released an estimate in June, finding that fully eliminating fares would cost New York State roughly $1.1 billion. Even so, Mamdani said he believes the designs will ultimately be fulfilled. "I continue to be excited at the work of making the slowest buses in America fast and free. And I appreciate the governor’s continued partnership in delivering on that agenda of affordability," Mamdani said at a news conference earlier this month. His term runs through Jan. 1, 2030. Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

articles.title: Sari-to-Salwar Switch: BJP walks away with Congress pick, wins Brij pradhan post
articles.summary: Brij Nagar Panchayat Samiti: Bati Kumari filed nominations for Congress, BJP and as independent, then withdrew two and won pradhan unopposed on BJP symbol; ex-MLA Wajib Ali resigned.
articles.body: Alwar: A weird political episode unfolded in Brij Nagar Panchayat Samiti in Deeg district during the indirect election for pradhan held Friday, when Congress and BJP ended up backing the same candidate—Bati Kumari (28)—who filed three separate nomination papers declaring herself a nominee from both parties as well as an independent.With no rival nominations filed, the contest effectively turned into a procedural drama. Bati Kumari ultimately withdrew her Congress and independent nominations and was declared elected unopposed as pradhan on the BJP symbol.The sequence of events drew attention across the state for its unusual visuals and rapid political switch. Kumari first filed as a Congress candidate in the presence of former MLA Wajib Ali, wearing a sari and keeping her face covered with a veil. Soon after, she appeared again alongside minister of state for home Jawahar Singh Bedam, filed as a BJP candidate, and this time wore a salwar suit, again with her face covered. She also submitted a form as an independent before withdrawing two of the three nominations.Kumari was originally elected as an independent member from ward number 14 of Brij Nagar Panchayat Samiti last Friday. In the newly elected panchayat samiti, Congress was poised to win the pradhan post in the indirect election as it had 16 members compared to BJP’s four, while nine others were independent. Despite having a majority in the 29-member panchayat samiti, Congress picked an independent as its candidate, leaving many in the party perplexed.When the result was declared and it surfaced that Kumari had clandestinely switched sides from Congress to BJP, former MLA Wajib Ali, who played a key role in her selection as a Congress candidate, resigned as a Pradesh Congress Committee (PCC) member on moral grounds within hours.Ali alleged misuse of power and money by BJP and claimed the candidate was “taken away,” remarking that the switch was accompanied by a change of clothes. The ex-MLA said, “People had voted for Congress in panchayat polls, but BJP wrote a script of deceit and fraud Wednesday.” He added, “The candidate had come with us wearing a sari, but this govt stooped so low, and the minister (Bedam) fell so low, that to win an election her clothes were changed. They did not win with people’s votes, they did not win in a democratic way. Just like a skit on a stage, the election was won by changing costumes. This is the real ‘vote theft’.”BJP district president Satish Bansal, on the other hand, described the development as the party’s splendid victory. “Bati Kumari filed her nomination as BJP candidate and won unopposed. articles.summary: Powerful NY Democrat Andrea Stewart-Cousins dead at 76, reports say
articles.body: Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the majority leader of the New York State Senate, has died at age 76, according to multiple reports. Stewart-Cousins, the first Black woman to lead the state's upper chamber, was found dead in her Yonkers home on Friday morning, police sources told the New York Post. Her daughter reportedly tried to get in touch with her on Thursday night before calling for a welfare check. Stewart-Cousins, a Democrat, was first elected to the state senate in 2007. She then became majority leader in January 2019 after Democrats won a majority in the chamber in the 2018 midterm elections. The Business Council of New York State issued this statement: "We are deeply saddened to learn of the sudden passing of Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins. As the first woman to lead a conference in the New York State Legislature, she made history and will forever be remembered for her strong leadership and dedication to New Yorkers. "A partner to The Business Council, Andrea was always willing to listen to employers and work toward common ground on behalf of the business community. We extend our deepest condolences to her family, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time," the statement said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This is a developing story. articles.body:
Thousands of households in the U.S. were without power on Black Friday after storms hit both the Northeast and West Coast on Thanksgiving.

Roughly 490,000 customers were without power as of Friday afternoon, according to tracking website PowerOutage.us . That included nearly 201,000 in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, about 69,500 in Missouri, roughly 60,000 in Maryland and more than 40,000 in New York, where the storms had postponed the famous Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday.

Power outages on Thanksgiving peaked at 940,000 customers, NBC News reported — citing data from PowerOutage.us .

Airlines have delayed nearly 1,950 flights within, into or out of the U.S. so far Friday, according to flight tracking site FlightAware . Airlines have also cancelled nearly 130 U.S. flights, although it is unclear what percentage of the delayed and cancelled flights were impacted by weather.

Conditions across the Eastern part of the country will “begin to improve” on Friday, the National Weather Service’s (NWS) prediction center said in an early morning statement.

“Seasonably cool temperatures will be felt across the Southeast in wake of the storm system before moderating this weekend,” the NWS said. “Rounds of rain along the coastline and valleys and locally heavy snow in high terrain will occur across the Pacific Northwest and portions of the northern Rockies Friday and Saturday.”

A storm system that moved from Florida through the Carolinas and to the Northeast brought inclement weather again on Friday, the service added. The system brought wet snow as far south as the Tennessee Valley.

articles.title: Pedro Almodóvar irrumpe en el cierre de campaña del PSOE con una petición: "Ya sabéis lo que tenemos que hacer el domingo"
articles.standfirst: El cineasta respalda a Pedro Sánchez en la Caja Mágica reivindicando la Memoria Democrática
articles.summary: El cineasta respalda a Pedro Sánchez en la Caja Mágica reivindicando la Memoria Democrática
articles.body: El cierre de campaña del PSOE en la Caja Mágica tuvo este viernes un marcado acento cultural e histórico con la participación de Pedro Almodóvar. El cineasta subió al escenario para recitar el poema No quiero, de Ángela Figuera Aymerich, y dar paso a Ángela Raya, nieta del sindicalista y dirigente socialista granadino José Raya, asesinado en agosto de 1936. Almodóvar puso en valor la perseverancia familiar para localizar al represaliado: "Durante décadas, su familia vivió sin saber dónde descansaban sus restos. Ángela convirtió ese dolor en una búsqueda de verdad y reparación". Tras 89 años de espera, el 19 de diciembre de 2025 lograron finalmente exhumarlo gracias a los fondos estatales y de la Junta de Andalucía. Para el director de cine, esta exhumación representa "la historia de tres generaciones que se negaron a olvidar" y demuestra la utilidad real de la legislación vigente en materia de Memoria Democrática. Ante el auditorio socialista, Almodóvar lanzó un claro aviso electoral frente a una posible alternancia política: "Tanto el PP como Vox han anunciado su intención de derogar la Ley de Memoria Democrática. Así que ya sabéis lo que tenemos que hacer el domingo". A continuación, tomó la palabra Ángela Raya, quien abogó por mantener viva la dignidad de las víctimas asegurando que "queremos seguir escribiendo un libro de luz" sobre la Guerra Civil y la dictadura. Con gran emoción, reivindicó la figura pacífica de su abuelo frente al relato revisionista: "Mi abuelo era tipógrafo. Le gustaba la tipografía y llevaba un sacapuntas. No lo fusilaron, lo ejecutaron, lo asesinaron. Entiendo que fusilar es otra cosa". Raya subrayó que "él solo tenía como arma la palabra, el amor, la generosidad" y zanjó cualquier duda sobre la veracidad histórica afirmando que "todo está documentado y escrito" y que "no es una invención como dicen algunos". La jornada electoral había arrancado previamente con la llegada de Pedro Sánchez junto a su esposa, Begoña Gómez, al ritmo de Dime que me quieres y Salta conmigo, interpretados por Alejo Stivel. Tras un vídeo conmemorativo de los ocho años de Ejecutivo progresista y la actuación de Alice Wonder, una locución definió el encuentro como "un homenaje a la cultura sin permitir que nadie, nunca más, vuelva a silenciarnos". En el tramo inicial también intervino el candidato al Senado por Madrid, Antonio Hernando, quien pidió apoyo para un "Senado de progreso" que "no sea donde se hagan comisiones inquisitoriales para perseguirnos, para impedir que los herederos que votaron la Constitución a regañadientes paren las instituciones desde atrás". El despliegue orgánico del partido acompañó el acto desde las primeras filas, ocupadas por los ministros del Gobierno, la presidenta Cristina Narbona, la secretaria de Organización Rebeca Torró y el exjefe de la diplomacia europea Josep Borrell. En las gradas posteriores se dieron cita diputados, senadores y figuras veteranas como José Bono y José Blanco, además de antiguos responsables institucionales y de comunicación como Ion Antolín, Francesc Vallès y Francisco Martín.
